statement: Adjustable positive linear regulator built on an LM317: the 1.25 V reference between OUT and ADJ is impressed across program resistor R1 so R2 sets Vout; Cin (~0.1 uF) is required when the regulator sits far from the power source, Cout (0.1 uF or larger) suppresses output voltage spikes, and a 10 uF ADJ-bypass capacitor raises ripple rejection from ~65 dB to ~80 dB.
condition: Positive adjustable rail from unregulated DC up to 37 V; input must stay at least ~2 V above the regulated output (standard 78xx/LM317 dropout), or ~0.5 V for an LDO alternative such as LM2940.
inputs: Unregulated DC, up to 37 V max (LM317)
outputs: Regulated positive DC set by R1/R2, up to 1.5 A max output current
required_blocks: LM317 3-terminal adjustable positive regulator (floating; sees only input-output differential)
R1 program resistor OUT-to-ADJ carrying the nominal 1.25 V reference
R2 output-set resistor ADJ-to-GND (increasing R2 raises Vout)
Cin ~0.1 uF at input pin, required if regulator is far from the power source
Cout ~0.1 uF or larger at output to eliminate voltage spikes
Optional 10 uF capacitor bypassing the ADJ divider: ripple rejection 65 dB -> ~80 dB
design_notes: Negative rail: complementary LM337 (-1.2 V to -37 V, 1.5 A max).
Higher voltage: TL783 regulates 1 to 125 V but only 700 mA max.
LDO regulators (see LM2940) cut required headroom from ~2 V to ~0.5 V, allowing lower Vin and cooler operation.
Upstream source voltage should not be much larger than the regulator output, or the regulator is forced to dissipate the excess as heat.
Fixed-output alternative: LM78xx series (7805..7824, 1.5 A heat-sunk); SMD SOT-89 versions often have lower max output current.

source.book: Practical Electronics for Inventors, 4th Ed. (Scherz & Monk)
source.section: 11.1.2 Adjustable-Regulator ICs; 11.1.3 Regulator Specifications; 11.6 Ripple Reduction

statement: Simplest battery-reversal protection: a series diode in the positive lead between battery (or external plug/jack) and load conducts only when the battery is installed correctly and blocks current from a backward-installed battery. The diode must be rated for the full load current; a low-threshold Schottky (~0.4 V) loses less headroom than a silicon diode (~0.6 V).
condition: Battery-powered or external-DC (plug-and-jack) equipment where reverse installation or reversed supply polarity is possible; acceptable to lose one diode drop of supply voltage.
inputs: Battery pack or external DC adapter input of either polarity
required_blocks: Series diode in the positive supply lead, rated for full load current (Schottky preferred, ~0.4 V drop; silicon ~0.6 V)
design_notes: The forward drop shortens battery operating time - about 0.6 V is lost immediately with silicon.
Best first-line design is a mechanical block preventing reverse installation; the diode guards against momentary fumbled contact.
For essentially zero voltage drop plus thermal shutdown and voltage monitoring, use dedicated protection ICs or transistor arrangements.
Note: many consumer DC barrel plugs are center-positive, but musical equipment (guitar pedals) is often center-negative - protection matters for external jacks too.

source.book: Practical Electronics for Inventors, 4th Ed. (Scherz & Monk)

statement: Choosing among reverse-polarity protection schemes: mechanical keying first, then series diode (simple, lossy), parallel shunt diode (no series drop, only for high-output-impedance batteries), or protection ICs/transistor circuits (near-zero drop with extra features).
condition: Any battery-powered or externally powered design where reverse insertion or reversed adapter polarity can occur, especially single-cell AA-alkaline, NiCad, or NiMH systems.
conditions: Mechanical block against reverse installation: best baseline design in all cases
Series diode: simplest electrical protection; use when losing ~0.6 V (Si) or ~0.4 V (Schottky) is acceptable
Parallel (shunt) diode: use with batteries that have high output impedance (e.g., alkaline cells) when the series drop must be eliminated
Protection IC or transistor arrangement: sophisticated designs needing essentially zero voltage drop, plus reverse-polarity protection, thermal shutdown, and voltage-level monitoring
tradeoffs: Series diode must carry the full load current and wastes one forward drop of battery voltage (shorter runtime)
Shunt diode eliminates the series drop and protects the load, but draws high current from a backward-installed battery
Protection ICs add cost/complexity but bundle zero-drop protection with monitoring features
failure_modes: Reverse current from a backward-installed cell can damage the circuit or the battery if not limited
Underrated shunt diode overheats: it must be properly rated for the current and power of a reversed low-impedance source
Series silicon diode may starve low-voltage loads (0.6 V lost immediately)

source.book: Practical Electronics for Inventors, 4th Ed. (Scherz & Monk)

statement: Linear regulators (78xx/LM317/LDO) are simplest and quietest but dissipate the input-output difference as heat (efficiency typically under 50%); switching regulators exceed 85% efficiency, can step down, step up, or invert, but put tens of millivolts of switching ripple on the output and need more parts.
condition: Choosing the regulation topology for a DC rail given input source, load current, efficiency/thermal budget, and output noise sensitivity.
conditions: Linear: input available at least 2-3 V above output (~0.5 V for LDO), low output noise required, minimal part count (a 7805 needs only input/output caps)
Switcher: efficiency, heat, or size is critical; also when output must be higher than input (step-up) or opposite polarity (inverting)
Off-line SMPS: mains-powered designs where the heavy 60 Hz transformer must be eliminated (high-frequency transformer, e.g. 65 kHz oscillator, is far smaller)
Prefer higher-switching-frequency regulator ICs: they use smaller inductors and reduce cost
tradeoffs: Linear power-conversion efficiency is typically lower than 50 percent - more than half the power becomes heat; switchers exceed 85 percent

Switcher output carries switching ripple typically in the tens of millivolts: acceptable against ~200 mV digital noise margins, but sensitive analog circuits may need an added external high-current low-pass filter
Part count: an LM2575-based 5 V switcher needs about six components vs three for a 7805
A 500 W switching supply occupies ~640 in3 vs ~1520 in3 for an equivalent linear supply (0.9 W/in3 vs 0.4 W/in3)
failure_modes: Linear regulator overheats when the source voltage is much higher than the regulated output (energy wasted as heat)
Regulation lost when input sags below Vout + dropout (2-3 V standard, ~0.5 V LDO)
Transformerless off-line switcher loses mains isolation - the DC input bus sits at ~160 V; isolation must be restored with a high-frequency transformer and optoisolator/transformer feedback

source.book: Practical Electronics for Inventors, 4th Ed. (Scherz & Monk)

statement: Give every device its own fuse rated about 50 percent above the expected nominal current, placed in series before the device (in the hot/black conductor for 120 VAC equipment); choose time-lag (slow-blow) fuses for motor/inductive circuits with large turn-on currents and fast-acting fuses elsewhere.
condition: Any line- or supply-powered device; the building's 15 A breaker protects house wiring only and will not save device electronics from an internal fault.

values.subminiature_pcb: 0.05 to 10 A, two wire leads, PCB mount

design_notes: The 50% margin also compensates for fuse current ratings that decrease as fuses age and for slight current variations.
Fast-acting fuses open on just a brief surge; time-lag types ride through inrush (motors, inductive loads).
Failure mode: a fuse or breaker placed in the neutral (white) line leaves the full line voltage present at the equipment input even after it blows.

source.book: Practical Electronics for Inventors, 4th Ed. (Scherz & Monk)

statement: Condition: supply is switched off while the capacitance on the regulator's output discharges more slowly than the capacitance on its input. Consequence: the regulator (e.g., 7805) becomes reverse-biased and the reverse-current surge from the load side can damage or destroy it.
condition: Linear regulator with significant output-side capacitance (bulk output caps or capacitive load) that can outlast the input capacitance at power-down.

values.fix_part: protection diode across the regulator (output to input), e.g., 1N400x class rectifier

design_notes: Fix: a diode wired from output to input across the regulator diverts the unwanted reverse current away from it.
A dual-diode arrangement - one diode output-to-input, a second from ground to output - also prevents attached loads from sending damaging spikes back into the IC's output.

source.book: Practical Electronics for Inventors, 4th Ed. (Scherz & Monk)
source.section: 11.5 A Few Simple Power Supplies (Fig 11.9); 4.2.5 (Fig 4.18 note)

statement: Condition: regulator IC used without its input/output capacitors (or without Cin when mounted far from the power source). Consequence: input and output spikes/noise are not removed, and high-frequency noise generated by the load appears on the regulated rail, eroding the ~200 mV noise margin of digital logic and risking false triggering.
condition: Any 78xx/79xx/LM317-class regulator application; Cin mandatory when the regulator is far from the upstream source, Cout always recommended.

values.cin: ~0.1 uF (needed when regulator far from power source)
values.cout: 0.1 uF or larger (eliminates output voltage spikes)
values.digital_noise_margin: ~200 mV minimum around critical logic levels
values.output_variation_budget_5v_digital: no more than 5 percent (0.25 V) on a 5 V rail

design_notes: Capacitors attached to the regulator's input and output terminals remove unwanted input or output spikes/noise (78xx series).
The output cap placed across the regulator output also bypasses high-frequency noise that the load itself generates.
Small analog signal circuits can require output variation under 1 percent - stricter than digital.

source.book: Practical Electronics for Inventors, 4th Ed. (Scherz & Monk)

statement: Worked sizing of the reservoir capacitor and regulator for a 5 V, 1.0 A full-wave-rectified supply: 4700 uF alone leaves 510 mV rms ripple (too much for a 0.25 V digital budget), but a 7805's ~60 dB ripple rejection divides it by 1000 to 0.51 mV; headroom then dictates a ~12 V transformer secondary.
problem: Keep the output variation of a 5 V digital supply within 5 percent (0.25 V) at a maximum load current of 1.0 A, using a full-wave rectifier front end.
assumptions: Full-wave rectification of 60 Hz mains gives 120 Hz ripple; period 1/120 Hz = 8.3 ms, of which ~5 ms is capacitor discharge and ~3.3 ms recharge
Straight-line (linear) discharge approximation replaces the exponential decay
Simplified formula form used in the text: Vr(rms) = 0.0024 s x I / C (e.g., 0.0024 s x (1.5 A / 4700 uF) = 760 mV)
steps: Compute raw ripple for C = 4700 uF at I = 1.0 A: Vripple(rms) = 510 mV - exceeds the 0.25 V budget
Do not chase a bigger capacitor: power-supply electrolytics have 5-20 percent (or worse) tolerance, so fine-tuning C is futile
Apply the regulator's ripple rejection instead: 7805 at ~60 dB attenuates ripple by a factor of 1000, giving 0.51 mV output ripple
Check headroom: the 7805 needs a minimum 3 V input-output differential, so Vin >= 8 V; add the 1-2 V rectifier drop and choose a transformer secondary of about 12 V
Adjustable variant: LM317 with C = 4700 uF at 1.5 A gives 760 mV raw ripple; with a 10 uF ADJ bypass its rejection rises from ~65 dB to ~80 dB (factor 10,000), leaving 0.076 mV
result: 4700 uF reservoir + 7805 fed from a ~12 V secondary yields ~0.5 mV output ripple on the 5 V rail, well inside the 0.25 V digital budget; the LM317 variant achieves 0.076 mV.
design_notes: Add a bleeder resistor (1 kOhm, 1/2 W suits most applications) across the unregulated output to discharge the high-voltage filter capacitor at power-off.
An RC snubber across the transformer primary (typical: 100 Ohm + 0.1 uF 1 kV) suppresses inductive turn-off transients.

source.book: Practical Electronics for Inventors, 4th Ed. (Scherz & Monk)
source.section: 11.6 Technical Points about Ripple Reduction; 11.7 Loose Ends

statement: Rectifier reservoir/filter capacitor: use a large electrolytic, typically 1000 uF or more, targeting a ripple factor (rms ripple / average DC) of about 0.05 or lower; check ESR, voltage, and ripple-current ratings, and parallel capacitors to reach higher capacitance.
condition: Capacitor-input filtering after a half-wave, full-wave, or bridge rectifier feeding a DC load or downstream regulator.

values.example: 1000 uF with 100 Ohm load, full-wave bridge: 0.34 VAC rms ripple, 1.17 V peak-to-peak, ripple factor 0.00251
values.half_wave_penalty: half-wave rectifier doubles the ripple voltage vs full-wave

design_notes: Electrolytics are used because other capacitor families cannot supply the needed microfarads (oil-filled types for high-voltage/high-current supplies).
Increasing load resistance (decreasing load current) also lowers ripple.
A downstream voltage-regulator IC between filter cap and load adds ripple rejection and holds the output constant against AC-line surges and load-current changes.

source.book: Practical Electronics for Inventors, 4th Ed. (Scherz & Monk)

statement: Place a 0.01-0.1 uF multilayer ceramic decoupling capacitor (rated >5 V) directly across the VCC-to-ground pins of each logic IC, as close to the IC as possible, to absorb the sharp supply-current spikes generated during totem-pole output transitions.
condition: Digital/logic systems where multiple devices share a supply rail; spikes otherwise cause false triggering of neighboring devices and electromagnetic radiation.

values.density: one capacitor per five to ten gates, or one per five counter/register ICs

design_notes: Close placement keeps current spikes local instead of letting them propagate back toward the power supply.
Related rule: never let unused CMOS inputs float - tie them high or low - and never drive CMOS inputs with the supply removed (damages input protection diodes).

source.book: Practical Electronics for Inventors, 4th Ed. (Scherz & Monk)

statement: To protect a load if the series regulator fails shorted, place a crowbar (zener + SCR) or a clamp (zener + high-power transistor) across the regulated output: the crowbar latches and diverts current to ground until power is cycled, while the clamp diverts current only while the overvoltage persists and ignores brief spikes.
condition: Regulated supply output where an internal regulator short would present the full unregulated input voltage to the load.
conditions: Crowbar: hard, latching shutdown wanted; trips when supply exceeds the zener breakdown by 0.6 V, firing the SCR
Clamp: use where voltage spikes would otherwise cause nuisance (false) crowbar triggering - the clamp needs no reset
Bare zener across the output: only for small fault currents
tradeoffs: Crowbar SCR stays conducting until the supply is switched off or its anode-cathode current is interrupted (needs reset); clamp recovers on its own
Clamp transistor diverts the excess current so the zener itself does not have to absorb it
failure_modes: A zener alone across the output can burn out ('fry') if the unregulated fault current is too large - add the power transistor to carry the current
Crowbar false-triggered by a transient spike takes the system down until reset

source.book: Practical Electronics for Inventors, 4th Ed. (Scherz & Monk)
